hints: Look carefully at the two curves, Q starts less steep than P but finishes higher, so think about what that tells you about rate and total amount.

Work out the moles in the first experiment, 0.100 mol of $\text{MgCO}_3$ with $0.0500 \text{ dm}^3 \times 1.00 \text{ mol dm}^{-3} = 0.050$ mol of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, and decide which reactant limits the $\text{CO}_2$ formed.
For Q you need slower initial rate but more $\text{CO}_2$ overall, so you need a lower $\text{H}^+$ concentration but a larger total number of moles of $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
**Read the graph like a chemist**

The steepness at the start tells you the initial rate. Q is less steep than P, so Q is slower.

The final flat level tells you the total volume of $\text{CO}_2$. Q finishes higher than P, so Q makes more gas.

**Find the limiting reactant in experiment P**

The equation is:
$$\text{MgCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Moles of acid in P $= 0.0500 \times 1.00 = 0.050$ mol. You have 0.100 mol of $\text{MgCO}_3$, but only 0.050 mol of acid in a 1:1 reaction, so acid is in excess of carbonate? No, acid is limiting. Only 0.050 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ can form.

**Translate Q into moles and rate**

To get more $\text{CO}_2$ you must provide more $\text{H}^+$ in total so that more carbonate can react. To get a slower rate at the same temperature you must lower the $\text{H}^+$ concentration.

Original $\text{H}^+$ total $= 2 \times 0.050 = 0.10$ mol from diprotic $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, with high concentration about $2.00 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

**Test the new acid**

$200 \text{ cm}^3$ of $1.00 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{HCl}$ gives:
$$n(\text{HCl}) = 0.200 \times 1.00 = 0.200 \text{ mol}$$
That is 0.200 mol of $\text{H}^+$, double the original total, and $[\text{H}^+] = 1.00 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, lower than before. Lower concentration gives slower start, larger total $\text{H}^+$ lets all 0.100 mol $\text{MgCO}_3$ react to give 0.100 mol $\text{CO}_2$. That is exactly curve Q.

options.A: Moles $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = 0.100 \times 0.500 = 0.050$ mol, identical to P. Total $\text{H}^+$ is the same, so final $\text{CO}_2$ volume would be the same, not higher. The lower concentration would slow the rate, but the plateau would not rise.
options.B: Moles $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = 0.100 \times 1.00 = 0.100$ mol, so more $\text{CO}_2$ could form. However the acid concentration is the same or higher than P, so the initial rate would be the same or faster, not slower as Q shows.
options.C: Moles $\text{HCl} = 0.200 \times 0.500 = 0.100$ mol. Since $\text{MgCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, 0.100 mol $\text{HCl}$ makes only 0.050 mol $\text{CO}_2$, same as P. Rate would be slower, but final volume would not increase.
options.D: Moles $\text{HCl} = 0.200 \times 1.00 = 0.200$ mol, giving 0.200 mol $\text{H}^+$. This reacts with all 0.100 mol $\text{MgCO}_3$ ($2:1$ ratio) to give 0.100 mol $\text{CO}_2$, double that in P, so plateau is higher. $[\text{H}^+] = 1.00 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ is lower than in P sulfuric acid, so initial rate is slower. This matches Q perfectly.
